title: JavaScript Is Single-Threaded
subtitle: One call stack per realm; async delegates to the host

cards.front: Single-threaded JS — precise claim?
cards.meaning: Per realm (tab main world, Worker, Node isolate): one JS call stack; at most one JS turn runs at a time. Sync code runs to completion before queued callbacks for that realm start.

cards.front: Why does this unit matter for event-loop / Promise questions?
cards.meaning: It is the foundation for the event loop, Promises, and async/await. If you get single-thread + host delegation wrong, every “predict the output” question becomes memorization instead of reasoning.

cards.front: Does single-threaded JS mean the browser/Node has one OS thread?
cards.meaning: No. It does not mean the whole browser or Node process has only one OS thread. Host work can use other OS threads; the claim is about one JS call stack per realm.

cards.front: Can network/disk/crypto use background threads?
cards.meaning: Yes. The single-thread claim does not mean network, disk, or crypto never use background threads. Waiting and some host work happen outside the JS thread.

cards.front: Main-thread JS vs host concurrency vs parallel JS — phrasing?
cards.meaning: User JavaScript on the main thread is single-threaded. Concurrency of waiting and some host work happens outside that thread; concurrency of JS computation needs Workers (or multiple processes).

cards.front: What is the JS call stack?
cards.meaning: The LIFO structure of function frames currently executing. While c runs inside b inside a, the stack is roughly a → b → c. When c returns, frames pop until the stack is empty for that turn of work.
cards.example: function a() { b(); } function b() { c(); } function c() { console.log('c'); } a();

cards.front: When can a queued callback start?
cards.meaning: Only when the engine is ready to start a new turn — which requires the stack from the previous turn to be empty. Nothing interleaves into the middle of a running function unless that function itself yields (e.g. await).

cards.front: Does await pause the JS thread like an OS blocking wait?
cards.meaning: No. await schedules continuation for later rather than pausing the thread like an OS blocking wait inside the JS engine. The current turn can finish; the continuation runs on a later turn of the same thread.

cards.front: Does async mean another JS thread?
cards.meaning: No. Async hands waiting work (timers, I/O, network) to the host (Web APIs, libuv), returns immediately, and runs callbacks later on the same JS thread when the stack is empty and the event loop picks them.

cards.front: What happens when you call setTimeout / fetch / fs.readFile?
cards.meaning: You are not starting another JS thread that sits and waits. (1) JS calls a host API. (2) The host registers work. (3) The JS call returns immediately; the stack continues. (4) Later the host queues a callback/task/microtask. (5) The event loop runs that callback on the same single JS thread when allowed.

cards.front: log start; setTimeout(0); log end — order?
cards.meaning: start, end, then timeout. setTimeout only schedules; sync code in the same turn finishes first; callback runs in a later turn after stack clears (and after microtasks for that phase).
cards.example: console.log('start'); setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0); console.log('end'); // start, end, timeout

cards.front: Non-blocking I/O in one sentence?
cards.meaning: JS thread doesn't sit waiting on slow I/O; host waits and enqueues callback when ready — many operations in flight, JS callbacks still serialized.

cards.front: Non-blocking I/O vs concurrent requests vs parallel JS?
cards.meaning: Non-blocking I/O: JS thread is not stuck waiting on slow I/O; host waits. Concurrent requests: many host operations in flight at once. Parallel JS on the main thread is false — still one stack. Parallel JS with Workers: separate stacks; communicate via messages.

cards.front: Where does concurrency happen if not JS stack?
cards.meaning: Browser Web APIs and rendering machinery; Node libuv/OS for I/O and thread pool ops. Many waits run elsewhere; your callback still runs single-threaded when it fires.

cards.front: Where does browser concurrency live, and why does a blocked main thread jank?
cards.meaning: Web APIs: timers, fetch/networking, DOM events, setTimeout, encoding, some crypto, etc. Rendering and compositing use other browser machinery; a blocked main JS thread still starves input handlers and often janks painting because those compete for the main thread's event loop turns.

cards.front: Where does Node concurrency live?
cards.meaning: libuv (+ OS APIs): network I/O, timers, filesystem (often via thread pool for some ops), DNS, etc. Your JS callbacks still serialize on the Node event loop thread unless you use worker_threads.

cards.front: Mental diagram of JS vs host vs queues?
cards.meaning: Your JS (one call stack) schedules work on the host (Web APIs / libuv / OS). When ready, the host enqueues a callback onto task/microtask queues. The event loop picks next work and runs it on the same single JS stack. The host may use threads; your callback still runs single-threaded JS when it finally runs.

cards.front: Why does a 3s busy while loop delay setTimeout(0)?
cards.meaning: Timer may fire in host time but JS callback can't start until the stack empties. Busy loop keeps stack occupied — UI/Node handlers starve even if timers are due.

cards.front: While a heavy loop occupies the stack, what cannot run?
cards.meaning: No other JS callback on that realm can run. Timer callbacks due “now” wait in queues. In the browser, event handlers, React updates scheduled as tasks, and often paint stay delayed → frozen UI. In Node, other request handlers on that loop wait → latency spikes under CPU-bound work.

cards.front: start; setTimeout(0); 3s busy loop; end — order?
cards.meaning: start, end, then (after ~3s of blocking) timer. The timer's delay elapsed long ago; the callback could not start until the stack emptied.
cards.example: console.log('start'); setTimeout(() => console.log('timer'), 0); while (Date.now() < end) {} console.log('end');

cards.front: Practical consequences of long sync CPU?
cards.meaning: Prefer async I/O over sync readFileSync on servers. Break huge CPU work: chunking, requestIdleCallback/scheduling, Workers, or native addons. In React/RN, expensive sync work in render/effects blocks interactions. In NestJS, CPU-heavy work in a request handler blocks the event loop for other requests on that process.

cards.front: Why doesn't setTimeout(fn, 0) run immediately?
cards.meaning: Delay is minimum, not guarantee. Callback goes to timer/macrotask queue; loop runs it only with empty stack after current sync work — and after microtasks scheduled in that turn beat the next timer.

cards.front: What does 0ms on setTimeout actually mean?
cards.meaning: “As soon as the timer is eligible and the loop gets to that task,” not “next CPU instruction.” setTimeout never runs its callback synchronously, even with a 0ms delay. Any currently running synchronous code, including code after the setTimeout call itself, runs first.

cards.front: Do browsers/Node ever run setTimeout(0) inline?
cards.meaning: No. Browsers may clamp nested timers; Node has its own timer phases — still never “inline sync.”

cards.front: setTimeout(0); Promise.resolve().then(...); sync log?
cards.meaning: sync, then microtask, then timeout — preview of event-loop priority within one turn's aftermath.
cards.example: setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('microtask')); console.log('sync'); // sync, microtask, timeout

cards.front: Is setTimeout(0) before all Promise callbacks?
cards.meaning: No. Microtasks (Promise .then, queueMicrotask) scheduled in the same turn run before the next timer macrotask. setTimeout(0) is not “before all Promise callbacks.” Full rules belong in the event-loop unit.

cards.front: Workers and the single-thread story?
cards.meaning: Each Worker is a separate realm with its own single JS thread and stack; message-passing, not shared call stacks. Main-thread JS stays single-threaded; parallelism is another realm.

cards.front: What does a Worker not share with the main thread?
cards.meaning: Lexical scope and this. Browser: Worker, SharedWorker. Node: worker_threads, or multiple processes/cluster. Each has its own JS thread and stack (still single-threaded inside the worker). Talks via structured clone / transferable messages (or shared memory in advanced cases).

cards.front: Because Workers exist, is JS multi-threaded?
cards.meaning: Do not say that. Say: main-thread JS is single-threaded; parallelism is another realm. Each worker is still single-threaded JS inside itself.

cards.front: async functions run on another thread?
cards.meaning: No — same thread until await; await schedules continuation later on that thread, not OS blocking wait inside the engine like a sync loop.

cards.front: Does a pending fetch mean JS is waiting in the background as JS?
cards.meaning: No. The network stack waits; your .then waits in a queue. Host waiting is not another JS thread sitting in your function.

cards.front: Does single-threaded mean no concurrency?
cards.meaning: No. Many host operations can be in flight; JS callbacks are serialized. Concurrency of waiting is real; parallel JS on the same stack is not.

cards.front: Does creating a Promise parallelize CPU?
cards.meaning: No — work before first await is sync and blocking; Promise only models async completion and queues reactions.

cards.front: Long sync loop vs “the event loop is broken”?
cards.meaning: Don't blame the event loop when the real bug is a long sync loop. Queues cannot preempt running JS. A busy stack blocks every callback and the UI even if timers already fired.

cards.front: Closures vs single-threading — which vs when?
cards.meaning: Closures still decide which variables a callback sees when it eventually runs. Single-threading decides when that callback is allowed to run relative to other JS.

cards.front: Does await invent threads?
cards.meaning: No. await does not invent threads; it schedules continuations on this same model: one JS stack, host waits, callbacks/continuations queued for later turns.

cards.front: Single-thread + async — strong one-liner?
cards.meaning: One JS stack runs at a time; async APIs ask the host to wait and queue callbacks for later, so a busy stack blocks every callback and the UI even if timers already fired.
